title: Judah the Prince
hookLine: Rabbi Judah, called simply Rabbi, gathers the oral teaching into the Mishnah

cards: One word, with no name after it: Rabbi. That's how the Talmud can refer to Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, Judah the Prince. Just Rabbi.
Nasi means prince, or leader, and he led the Jewish community of his day. But his lasting work wasn't politics. It was a book.
For generations, the sages' teachings had been passed on by mouth, teacher to student, memorized and repeated. Rabbi gathered them and set them in order. The result is called the Mishnah.

teach.h: ORAL WORDS, NOT TO BE WRITTEN.
teach.b: Here's the tension. The rabbis had a rule, recorded in tractate Gittin: words given orally, you may not say from writing.
The Oral Torah was meant to live in memories, in the back and forth between teacher and student, and writing it down risked freezing it. So how could anyone write it down?

teach.h: A TIME TO ACT FOR THE LORD.
teach.b: The Talmud answers with a verse from the Psalms, read in a daring way: "It is time for the LORD to work; they have made void Thy law." There are times when, to protect the Torah, you have to do what is normally not done.
Maimonides gives Rabbi's reason: students were growing fewer, troubles kept coming, and teaching that lived only in memory could be lost. The tradition itself disagrees about exactly what Rabbi did.
Maimonides wrote that he compiled the Mishnah and wrote it down. Rashi held that he arranged it and fixed its wording, but that it was still learned by heart, and only written later.

Both agree on the heart of it: Rabbi gave the teaching an order. He didn't erase the arguments. The Mishnah keeps the house of Shammai beside the house of Hillel, names who said what, and records minority views.

And the Talmud remembers him as a person, not only an editor: a story in tractate Bava Metzia tells that he once spared a family of small animals his maid wanted to sweep away, quoting the psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works."

how: The Mishnah attributed to Rabbi Judah the Prince is the foundation text of the Talmud, studied in yeshivas, synagogues and homes, and some learners take a little each day.

games.q: you're Rabbi Judah. the oral teaching is meant to be spoken, but students are scattered and memories are fragile. what do you do?
o: keep it oral and hope it survives.
gather it and set it in order.
games.why: he gathers the teaching into the Mishnah, keeping the arguments and minority views. later rabbis explain such writing with a verse read as a time to act for the LORD.

practice: Picture one small thing in your life that's scattered: a pile of papers, a phone full of notes, a family recipe that lives only in one person's head.

Imagine it gathered and ordered, nothing important thrown out, every voice still in it, and let the first small step become clear. If you pray, you can offer that work as the rabbis offered their study.
